design_detail: Case series from the National Poisons Unit, Guy's Hospital, London. All enquiries to the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) London about suspected 'ecstasy' or MDMA use from January 1990 to December 1991 were recorded; clinical details and outcomes were requested from the hospital and, where appropriate, the pathologist or coroner; and the Unit's laboratory records were searched for samples in which 'ecstasy' was mentioned or detected (p. 385, Methods). Reported: monthly NPIS enquiries (figure); 7 deaths with analytical confirmation of MDMA (Table I); 5 survivors with severe complications (Table II); one person reported to have taken a large number of tablets, with a high plasma concentration and mild symptoms (text only); 5 people from 4 road traffic accidents in whom MDMA was detected, 2 of whom died (Table III); and 7 cases of liver injury after reported 'ecstasy' use, without analytical confirmation, 1 of whom died (Table IV). Plasma concentrations measured in the Unit's laboratory or, for fatal cases 1–4, in other laboratories. No denominator, no comparison group, no statistics.
can_establish: That in 1990–1991 enquiries to the London poisons information service about MDMA rose, and that a recognisable severe pattern (temperature 40–43°C, seizures, disseminated intravascular coagulation, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure) was recorded in 7 people aged 16–21 who died after reportedly taking 1 to 5 tablets, or an unstated number, at clubs, parties or a concert, with MDMA confirmed in each and plasma concentrations of 0.11–1.26 mg/l where measured, while one person who reportedly took far more had a much higher concentration (7.72 mg/l) and mild symptoms.
cannot_establish: How often MDMA use leads to death or severe toxicity (no count of people using it); that heat, dancing, crowding or fluid intake caused the deaths (none was recorded; the authors propose it); what plasma concentration is dangerous (sampling times unknown, hospital samples, no comparison group); that MDMA caused the liver injuries (not confirmed analytically in any of the 7, and other causes not fully excluded); or that MDMA caused the road accidents (presence only).

sample.recruitment: Cases came to the National Poisons Unit as telephone enquiries from hospitals to the NPIS London or as samples sent to its laboratory, January 1990 to December 1991; outcomes were requested from the hospitals and, where appropriate, pathologists or coroners (p. 385).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Table I: deaths with analytical confirmation of MDMA ingestion. Table II: 'severely symptomatic' cases, criteria not stated. Table III: people whose samples from the scene of four road traffic accidents contained MDMA. Table IV: liver injury associated with reported 'ecstasy' ingestion, criteria not stated. No rule is given for which enquiries were tabulated, and the number of enquiries with known outcomes is not reported.
sample.demographics: Deaths (Table I): 5 men and 2 women aged 16–21. Severe survivors (Table II): ages 1 (an accidental ingestion) to 25, 3 male and 2 female. Road traffic cases (Table III): 4 men and 1 woman aged 18–23. Liver injury (Table IV): 6 men and 1 woman aged 19–29.
sample.attrition: Not applicable; how many enquiries lacked outcome information is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Only cases in which a hospital called a poisons service or sent a sample to one laboratory, and of these mainly the most severe; the mild cases that the authors say made up most enquiries (p. 386) are not counted or described in numbers. Enquiry numbers reflect clinicians' use of the service as well as cases, so a rise in calls is not by itself a rise in harm. Deaths without a call or sample, and deaths outside hospital, are missed.

exposure.measurement: Reported tablets or capsules taken, as recorded in the case circumstances; plasma MDMA and other substances measured in the Unit's laboratory or, for fatal cases 1–4, in other laboratories (Table I footnote); MDA, a metabolite, cannot be told apart from co-ingested MDA in biological samples (p. 385). The time of sampling relative to ingestion or admission is not given, and the screening scope behind 'other drugs were not detected' is not described. Liver cases: reported use only, with no analytical confirmation because use had stopped (p. 386).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported intake as study data, tablet content unknown. Deaths: 3 tablets (case 1), 2 (2), 5 (3), 1 (4), 'tablets' (5), not stated (6), 3 (7). Survivors: 3 tablets, 1 tablet (a child, accidental), 2 tablets sold as amphetamine, 3 capsules, 2.5 tablets over 4.5 h. Plasma MDMA (mg/l): deaths 0.36, detected, detected (blood and urine), 0.424, 0.11, 1.16, 1.26; severe survivors 0.2, 0.7, 0.97, 0.24, 0.21; road traffic cases 0.1, 0.13, 0.05, 0.34, 0.15; the person with mild symptoms 7.72 (pp. 385–386).
exposure.polysubstance: Deaths: amphetamine at a low concentration in one (the footnote says case 5; the table places it, with MDA, in case 6) and no ethanol or other drugs detected in any. Severe survivors: amphetamine in cases 1 and 4, MDA in cases 3 and 4, MDEA in the urine of case 4; case 3 had taken tablets sold as amphetamine. Road traffic cases: MDA and amphetamine in cases 4 and 5, with ephedrine (and triprolidine in case 4) in urine; case 3 reportedly took alcohol, but ethanol was detected in none; an amyl nitrite bottle was found on case 5. Liver cases: psilocybe, cocaine and cannabis (case 1), LSD and cannabis (case 5) (Tables I–IV).

comparison.controls: None. The contrasts are inside the series: one person with a plasma concentration several times higher than any fatal case had only mild symptoms (p. 385), and the plasma values of the 8 people who survived in Tables II and III (0.05–0.97 mg/l) overlap those of the deaths in Table I (0.11–1.26 mg/l) (editors' comparison, pp. 385–386).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history is reported only in passing (haemophilia in fatal case 6; in the liver cases, no history of regular alcohol or injecting drug use and no evidence of paracetamol overdose). Physical activity, ambient temperature, clothing, fluid intake and time spent dancing are not recorded for any case (editors' observation from Tables I–II).

outcomes.instruments: Clinical course and outcome from hospital records and, where appropriate, pathologists or coroners: temperature, pulse, blood pressure, seizures, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, liver tests and hepatitis serology, treatment, time to death or discharge (Tables I–IV).
outcomes.operationalization: A death enters the 'fatal cases of MDMA toxicity' (Table I) with analytical confirmation of MDMA and the clinical course shown; the cause of death is the authors' reading ('probably' heatstroke with DIC, p. 386), and no certified cause, post-mortem finding or coroner's conclusion is reported. One of the 7 died of graft rejection 18 days after a liver transplant (Table I, case 5). 'MDMA hepatotoxicity' is jaundice or hepatitis after reported 'ecstasy' use with hepatitis A and B (and in 4 cases C) serology negative.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics. Editors' summaries from the tables: in the 5 deaths with a measured plasma MDMA, 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, against 7.72 mg/l in the person with mild symptoms; recorded temperatures in the deaths 40 to 43°C; deaths 2.5 h to 60 h after admission, plus one 18 days after a transplant. Enquiries (editors' approximate reading of the figure, no values printed): about 64 in 1990 and about 343 in 1991.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: the number of enquiries, how many had known outcomes and how many were mild; post-mortem findings or certified causes for any death; sampling times; and any detail of the person with 7.72 mg/l beyond one sentence.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A two-year series from one poisons service: rising enquiries about MDMA; 7 deaths in people aged 16–21 after reportedly taking a few tablets at clubs, parties or a concert, with temperatures of 40–43°C, seizures, DIC, rhabdomyolysis and renal failure, and plasma MDMA of 0.11–1.26 mg/l where measured; 5 severely ill survivors; one person with 7.72 mg/l and mild symptoms; 5 road traffic cases with MDMA present (2 died); and 7 liver injuries after reported use, none confirmed analytically (1 died).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports a recent increase in severe toxicity following recreational use of small amounts of MDMA (p. 384); the series shows more enquiries and laboratory detections, with no count of people using MDMA, and the amounts are reported tablets of unknown content. The discussion attributes the deaths 'probably' to heatstroke and proposes that sustained activity, high ambient temperature and inadequate fluid replacement at crowded venues add to a direct drug effect on thermoregulation (p. 386), citing animal studies; none of these was recorded in any case, so this is the authors' hypothesis, and the conclusion that the acute toxicity 'may be due mainly to the circumstances' of use (p. 387) rests on it. The liver injuries are presented as MDMA hepatotoxicity, although MDMA was not confirmed in any case and the authors themselves list a metabolite, a contaminant or an additive as possible causes (p. 386). The statement that all fatal cases were at crowded parties or clubs fits Table I except case 7 (a pop concert) and case 6 (found in the street after a party), and crowding is not recorded. The abstract counts 7 fatalities while the paper describes 10 deaths. The road traffic cases are presented neutrally as MDMA identified, which is what they show.

timeline.event: Brown & Osterloh reported multiple severe complications after recreational MDMA ingestion (JAMA; cited as reference 4; not read).
Chadwick et al. (1991) and Campkin & Davies (1992) reported single UK deaths with coagulopathy and hyperthermia; the paper marks its fatal cases 4 and 7 with these references (not read).

This series. Two Lancet letters in reply, named in the project's search log as reporting further complications (Rittoo et al., doi 10.1016/0140-6736(92)92261-d; Ellis, no DOI), are not among the files and were not read.
Milroy analysed MDMA concentrations in deaths attributed to MDMA toxicity against deaths from trauma (as described on the project's drug-deaths list; card written by another reader in this round).
Parrott reviewed the thermal effects of MDMA in humans (title as listed; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: A landmark early UK description of the hyperthermic pattern of fatal MDMA toxicity; a descriptive series, so replication in the usual sense does not apply. Its environmental explanation was a hypothesis here: the project's before-and-during list records that the evidence on heat and dancing is one laboratory study of room temperature, field surveys and reviews, with no trial of cooling, rest or chill-out areas (search-logs/BeforeDuring_DOI-LIST.md, section 11, Known gaps). Overlap between concentrations in fatal and non-fatal cases is taken up in later work (Milroy, 2011).

funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported (no conflict-of-interest statement). The acknowledgement thanks the doctors who provided details of patients and four named individuals for their help (p. 387).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the National Poisons Unit, Guy's Hospital, London (p. 384), which ran both the enquiry service and the laboratory from which the cases came.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective surveillance of people treated for MDMA toxicity with timed blood samples, analysis of any remaining tablets, and recorded setting, ambient temperature, activity and fluid intake, compared with people using MDMA in the same settings without harm, with a denominator of use from concurrent surveys; for the liver, analytically confirmed cases with full exclusion of other causes.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Calls to one poisons service and samples sent to one laboratory are not a frame for MDMA toxicity in the population.
No rule is given for which enquiries became tabulated cases; mild cases are not described.
7 deaths, 5 severe survivors, 5 road traffic cases and 7 liver cases; adequate to describe a pattern, not to estimate any frequency.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Each case has age, sex, circumstances, reported amount, clinical course, analytical results and outcome.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: The number of enquiries, and how many had known outcomes, is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: MDMA was analytically confirmed in the deaths and severe cases, but not in the liver cases; the road traffic cases show presence only; the cause of each death is the authors' reading, without post-mortem findings.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Analyses in different laboratories, sampling times not given, some results 'detected' without a concentration, hepatitis C serology missing in 3 liver cases.
Description suits a case series, but the claimed increase in severe toxicity rests on raw enquiry counts without a denominator.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Clinical details were requested from hospitals; how many responded is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison. The cases are clearly tabulated with analytical confirmation, but they were assembled from calls and samples sent to one poisons service, without inclusion rules, denominators, sampling times or any record of the circumstances the authors invoke, so the editors summarise the risk of bias as high for anything beyond description. It may be cited for: the clinical pattern recorded in the 7 deaths (temperature 40–43°C, seizures, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure); their settings and reported tablet numbers as recorded; the plasma MDMA concentrations in these cases alongside one higher concentration with mild symptoms, as an illustration that concentration and outcome did not line up; the 5 road traffic cases as presence of MDMA; and, attributed to the authors, the heat-and-exertion hypothesis. It may not be cited for a death rate, for heat, dancing or fluids causing the deaths, for a dangerous concentration, or for MDMA causing liver injury.

key_findings.finding: Methods: all enquiries to the NPIS London about suspected 'ecstasy' or MDMA use from January 1990 to December 1991 were recorded and collated; clinical details and outcomes were requested from the hospital and, where appropriate, the pathologist or coroner; and the National Poisons Unit laboratory records were searched for samples in which 'ecstasy' was mentioned or detected.

Enquiries were few until the second half of 1991, when a striking increase in calls was noted; laboratory detections of MDMA and MDA rose similarly, MDMA being found more often. What was sold as 'ecstasy' usually contained MDMA, but MDA or amphetamine were also identified; mixtures were uncommon.
key_findings.note: Editors' approximate reading of the figure bars (no values printed; 300-dpi crop): at most about 15 calls a month in 1990 (about 64 in the year), rising from February 1991 to about 51 in October 1991 (about 343 in 1991); the rise began in the first half of 1991 (about 124 calls) rather than only in the second (about 219).

key_findings.finding: Seven deaths with analytical confirmation of MDMA (Table I): 5 men and 2 women aged 16–21; reported intake 3 tablets in a club, 2 tablets at a party, 5 tablets at a party, 1 tablet in a club, 'tablets' at a party, not stated (a man with haemophilia found collapsed in the street after a party) and 3 tablets at a pop concert. Recorded temperatures 40°C to 43°C (41.8, 41, 42.1 within 4.5 h of ingestion, 40, 41, 40 and 43°C); seizures recorded in 5, DIC in 5, rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure in 3. Deaths 2.5 h to 60 h after admission (two at 14 h and 15.5 h after ingestion); one woman had a liver transplant after 4 days and died of graft rejection after 18 days.
key_findings.note: Table I is an image without a text layer; values read on 150-dpi renderings and 300-dpi crops. Counts are editors' tallies: seizures from two columns (case 4's seizure is recorded under circumstances, cases 2, 5, 6 and 7 under clinical course); DIC (cases 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7) and rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure (cases 5, 6 and 7) from the clinical-course column.

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations in the deaths (mg/l): MDMA 0.36 (case 1), detected (2), detected in blood and urine (3), 0.424 (4), 0.11 (5), 1.16 with MDA 0.06 and amphetamine 0.10 (6), 1.26 (7). Samples for cases 1–4 were analysed in other laboratories; the footnote says that, apart from a low concentration of amphetamine in case 5, ethanol and other drugs were not detected in any case.
key_findings.locator: Table I, analytical amounts column and footnote
key_findings.note: Read on the rendered page; the decimal points in 0.11 and 0.10 (and in 6.5 h for case 7) are not visible in the scan and were read by analogy with the other values. The amphetamine is in the row of case 6, not case 5 (reporting issues). Sampling times are not given.

key_findings.finding: One analytically documented overdose, of allegedly 42 tablets taken at home, with plasma MDMA 7.72 mg/l, was accompanied by no symptoms other than a 'hangover', with tachycardia and hypertension. The authors write that doses were difficult to establish but that in most cases only a few tablets or capsules seemed to have been taken, and the pattern of toxicity did not seem to result from overdose.
key_findings.locator: Results (single paragraph), left column continuing in the right column
key_findings.note: The OCR text layer reads '7-72 mg/1'; the printed page reads 7·72 mg/l (300-dpi crop). No age, sex, sampling time or other detail is given for this person.

key_findings.finding: Five survivors with severe complications (Table II): a man of 23 after 3 tablets in a club (convulsion, temperature 40°C, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure; MDMA 0.2 and amphetamine 0.1 mg/l; 20 days of veno-venous haemofiltration, 33 days in hospital); a boy recorded as aged 1 after accidentally swallowing 1 tablet (convulsions for 30 min; MDMA 0.7 mg/l; symptom-free by 6 h); a woman of 19 after 2 tablets sold as 'amphetamine' in a club (coma, temperature 39.7°C, thrombocytopenia; MDMA 0.97 and MDA 0.05 mg/l; recovered); a man of 20 after 3 capsules in a club (pulse 210, temperature 40°C, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure; MDMA 0.24, MDA 0.02, amphetamine 0.02 mg/l, MDEA in urine; 21 days in hospital); a woman of 25 after 2.5 tablets over 4.5 h at home (subarachnoid haemorrhage on CT; MDMA 0.21 mg/l; neurosurgery, full recovery).
key_findings.note: Table II is an image; values read on the rendered page, with decimal points in 0.2, 0.7 and 39.7 not visible in the scan.

key_findings.finding: Samples from the scenes of four road traffic accidents contained MDMA in 5 people (Table III): the driver (21, multiple fractures; MDMA 0.1 mg/l) and a passenger (23, multiple skull fractures; 0.13) of the same car in a head-on collision both died; a man of 21 who had taken 'ecstasy' and alcohol (0.05) discharged himself; a woman of 23 who denied drug use (0.34, with MDA, amphetamine, and ephedrine and triprolidine in urine) recovered fully; a pedestrian of 18 hit while staggering across a road, with an amyl nitrite bottle in his pocket (0.15, with MDA, amphetamine and ephedrine), was discharged after 11 days with a minor residual deficit. Ethanol was not detected in any.
key_findings.locator: Results (single paragraph), right column (p. 385); Table III and footnote (p. 386)

key_findings.finding: Seven cases of liver injury after reported 'ecstasy' use (Table IV; 6 men, 1 woman, aged 19–29): reported use from one tablet three weeks earlier to regular use for 3 or 10 months and escalating use to 4 tablets weekly; one fulminant hepatic failure treated by a successful liver transplant, one death (a man of 20 who had also used LSD and cannabis for 2 years, with encephalopathy, coagulopathy and adult respiratory distress syndrome), the others recovering or resolving. Hepatitis A IgM and hepatitis B surface antigen were negative in all, hepatitis C antibody negative in the 4 tested; liver biopsy in 2 showed eosinophilic infiltration. MDMA could not be confirmed analytically because use had stopped; the authors say whether MDMA, a metabolite, a manufacturing contaminant or a tablet additive was responsible was not yet clear.
key_findings.locator: Results (single paragraph), right column (p. 385); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 386); Table IV and footnote (p. 387)

key_findings.finding: Most cases on which the Unit was consulted had mild symptoms (agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, widely dilated pupils, trismus, sweating); the most severe were characterised by hyperthermia, DIC, rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure, and death was probably due to heatstroke with DIC. The authors note that this pattern can follow amphetamine sulphate overdose but had only recently been seen with MDMA in the UK, for reasons not clear.

The authors found no evidence that an impurity or manufacturing variation was responsible and suggested a combination of direct drug effects and circumstances: most serious and all fatal cases they encountered were among people at crowded parties or clubs, where sustained physical activity, a high ambient temperature and inadequate fluid replacement could all reduce heat loss and add to a direct effect on thermoregulation (citing animal studies in which hyperthermia is greater at high ambient temperature). On this basis they suggested early medical management with intravenous fluids and intravenous dantrolene, untested in the series, noting that their fatal cases already had established heatstroke when first seen, and speculated that some people developing severe toxicity may have a metabolic myopathy.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Activity, ambient temperature and fluid intake were not recorded for any case in Tables I–II (editors' observation).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that MDMA can cause severe toxicity and that its acute pattern in this series may be due mainly to the circumstances in which it is used; they argue for publicity because 'ecstasy' was widely seen as safe, for clinicians to include MDMA in the differential diagnosis of severe hyperthermia, for analytical confirmation in young people with behavioural disturbance or after accidents when circumstances suggest MDMA, and for hepatotoxicity to be recognised as a complication; the frequency and degree of long-term effects on the brain and mental function were unknown.

Editors' comparison across Tables I–III: plasma MDMA in the 8 people who survived (5 with severe complications, 0.2–0.97 mg/l; 3 after road accidents, 0.05, 0.15 and 0.34 mg/l) overlaps the range in the 5 deaths from MDMA toxicity with a measured value (0.11–1.26 mg/l); the 2 people who died of injuries in a road accident had 0.1 and 0.13 mg/l. All are plasma values from hospital or accident samples, not blood taken after death, and no sampling time is given for any.
key_findings.locator: Table I (p. 385); Tables II and III (p. 386)
key_findings.note: Values read on 150-dpi renders and 300-dpi crops; the decimal points in 0.2 and 0.7 (Table II) are not visible in the scan. The survivors were seen in hospital after severe complications or accidents, and one was a child of 1 who swallowed a tablet, so none of these values describes ordinary use without harm.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table I says the low amphetamine concentration was in case 5, but the table lists amphetamine 0.10 mg/l (with MDA 0.06) in the row of case 6; case 5 has MDMA only.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which death had amphetamine is uncertain; the table row is the more specific source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract counts 7 fatalities, but the paper describes 10 deaths: the 7 in Table I, the 2 road traffic deaths in Table III and the liver-injury death in Table IV.
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts of deaths involving MDMA drawn from this paper depend on which tables are used; the three other deaths are not discussed as deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: Table IV gives bilirubin in mmol/l (40 to 530), a unit in which these values would be impossible; µmol/l is presumably meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unit error; the bilirubin values should not be quoted with the printed unit.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says none of the liver cases had a history of heavy alcohol or intravenous drug use and none had evidence of infectious hepatitis, and that hyperthermic liver toxicity can be excluded; Table IV records past intravenous drug use (more than 5 years earlier) in case 4, reports no hepatitis C antibody result for cases 2, 5 and 7, and gives no temperatures.
reporting_issues.consequence: Other causes of the liver injuries were excluded less completely than the text states.

reporting_issues.issue: The text places the rise in enquiries in the second half of 1991, but the figure shows monthly calls rising from February 1991 (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the timing of the rise is earlier than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says all fatal cases were among people at crowded parties or clubs; Table I records a pop concert (case 7) and a person found in the street after a party (case 6), and crowding is not recorded for any case.
reporting_issues.consequence: The setting statement is a generalisation slightly beyond the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The case with plasma MDMA 7.72 mg/l and mild symptoms appears only in one sentence of the results, without age, sex, sampling time, clinical findings or any table entry.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's key contrast between concentration and outcome cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table III says ethanol was not detected in any case, while case 3 is recorded as having taken 'ecstasy' and alcohol.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a contradiction if the alcohol had been eliminated, but it shows that negative results depend on unreported sampling times.

verification.source_read: PDF of the scanned print pages, Lancet 340, pp. 384–387 (4 page images, all read; p. 384 begins with the end of a preceding article on atopy, not used). The OCR text layer covers only the running text; the figure and Tables I–IV are images and were read on 150-dpi renderings and 300-dpi crops, which are the source for every table and figure value. Some decimal points (printed as middle dots) are not visible in the scan and were read by analogy with the other values in the same column. No funding or conflict statement. The two Lancet letters in reply named in the project's search log (Rittoo et al., 10.1016/0140-6736(92)92261-d; Ellis, no DOI) are not among the files and were not read. The reference record agrees with the PDF (title, three authors, 1992, volume 340, pages 384–387; the issue number is not printed on these pages). Locators count running-text paragraphs within each section.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 331 (corrected): the counts are right only if both columns are used; seizures appear in the clinical-course column for cases 2, 5, 6 and 7 and in the circumstances column for case 4; DIC and rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure are in the clinical-course column.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking Table I on the rendered p. 385 (150 dpi; 300-dpi render for the values): case 4 'seizure' under circumstances, cases 2, 5, 6, 7 under clinical course; DIC in 2, 4, 5, 6, 7; rhabdomyolysis with ARF in 5, 6, 7. Note reworded; the finding's counts (5, 5, 3) are unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 331 (missed): Tables II and III against Table I: the five survivors of severe complications had plasma MDMA 0.2–0.97 mg/l and the two people who died of injuries in road accidents 0.1 and 0.13 mg/l, inside the range of the fatal toxicity cases (0.11–1.26 mg/l); the card holds the values but not the comparison.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted in substance after checking Tables I–III on rendered pp. 385–386 (300-dpi crops of the value columns): added as a key finding with the 3 road-accident survivors (0.05, 0.15, 0.34 mg/l) counted among the people who survived (8 in all, 0.05–0.97 mg/l). The road-accident deaths are given separately: 0.1 mg/l lies just below the lowest toxicity value, so 'inside the range' is not said of them. Also raised by the editor for this round.

disagreements.first_pass: None. The only contrast is inside the series: one person with a plasma concentration several times higher than any fatal case had only mild symptoms (p. 385).
